title: Amion Alternatives for Call Scheduling: What to Look At
description: Amion alternatives for residency call scheduling. What each tool is built for, and where handing the build to a service fits.
content:
Summary

  • Building a call schedule takes a chief resident hours they do not have, and someone is usually still unhappy with the result.
  • With most scheduling platforms, someone at the program configures the ACGME rules and checks the output, which takes time and expertise.
  • The real question when comparing Amion alternatives is who builds the schedule to the rules, not just where it is published.
  • Managed services like Scheduling Wizard take the build off the program by delivering finished schedules built to the ACGME requirements you tell us apply, saving programs dozens of hours a year.

Every year, a new cohort of chief residents inherits one of the most thankless jobs in medicine: building the call schedule. As one resident put it on Reddit, "it usually takes him 10-15 hours each quarter to make the schedule, and still everyone ends up pissed off about something." If you are looking at Amion alternatives because of that, the first thing to sort out is whether you need a better place to publish the schedule or someone to build it.

There are plenty of scheduling platforms to choose from, some built for healthcare broadly and some for shift work in general. Whichever you choose, someone has to put in the ACGME duty hour requirements, night float limits, PGY-level restrictions, continuity clinic protections and specialty rules that govern residency and fellowship training.

With a self-service tool, that someone is usually the chief resident or program coordinator.

What Amion Does Well, and Why Programs Look Further

Amion is where a lot of residency programs publish the call schedule, and for good reason. Residents already know it, it works on a phone, and it makes it easy to see who is on call and how to reach them. For a program that already has a reliable way to build the schedule, there may be no reason to change anything.

Programs usually start looking at alternatives for a different reason: building the schedule is still taking the chief weeks, the ACGME checks still happen by hand, and the knowledge of how it all fits together leaves every July. That is a question about who builds the schedule, not where it is published, and the options below answer it in different ways. Some of them replace the publishing step too; some, like ours, leave that choice to you.

A note before the list: we are Scheduling Wizard. We build physician schedules as a service, so we have included ourselves below and you should read our entry with that in mind. The order here is by one thing only, who actually builds the schedule, which is why a service comes first and the spreadsheet second; the software and the platforms you publish through follow. Rank by cost, or by how good the mobile app is, and the order changes. We have described the other tools as their own users and documentation describe them.

What Makes GME Scheduling Different

Most scheduling tool evaluations go wrong by treating GME scheduling as ordinary shift work.

Call scheduling to the ACGME rules involves more than keeping hours under 80 a week averaged over four weeks. It also involves:

  • Night float limits, where a Review Committee caps consecutive weeks or months of night float
  • Continuity clinic protections, ensuring residents aren't pulled from outpatient continuity clinics for inpatient call, even when coverage is short
  • Specialty rules, where each Review Committee adds its own requirements on supervision, clinic and call structure on top of the common hour limits
  • Inter-rotation dependencies, a call assignment downstream of a demanding rotation may violate rest rules even if it looks fine in isolation
  • PGY-level rules, certain rotations, call frequencies, and supervision requirements differ across training years

When these rules have to be configured and checked by the program, the administrative work stays with the program.

With that framework established, here's our evaluation of five tools, scored across three criteria:

  1. ACGME Rules: Built-in or manually configured?
  2. Compliance Checks: Automatic or requires human audit?
  3. Schedule Handling: Does the tool build the schedule, or publish one you built?

1. Scheduling Wizard

Model: Done-for-you managed scheduling service

Scheduling Wizard is the only entry on this list that operates as a fully managed service, meaning chief residents never have to touch scheduling software at all. Programs submit their rules (resident names, PGY levels, vacation requests, rotation rules), and receive the finished schedule, built to the ACGME requirements they tell us apply, delivered as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. It is backed by Y Combinator (W26) and built for GME first, and for provider groups and practices as well.

  • ACGME Rules: Built-In. The rules are not a configurable feature; they are written down with you and built into the schedule by our team. The subspecialty requirements you tell us apply, night float limits, continuity clinic protections and PGY-level rules all go in the same way, not layered on top by the user.
  • Compliance Checks: Built in. The schedule is built to the rules rather than audited against them afterwards. We still review it before it goes out; the review is a check, not a repair job.
  • Schedule Handling: Full build. Scheduling Wizard creates the schedule. It handles Block, Call, Clinic, and Attending schedules, balances fairness across residents, integrates preferences, and resolves cross-schedule conflicts in the build.

What is different: the operator role leaves the program. The chief resident does not configure rules or spend 10-15 hours a quarter in a spreadsheet, and reviews a finished schedule rather than building one. The written rule set also persists across annual chief rotations, meaning institutional knowledge doesn't walk out the door every July.

Whether you keep Amion is entirely up to you. Many programs upload our finished schedule into Amion or another platform they already use; others use the live view, or both.

What you get: the finished call schedule in the format your program asks for, Excel or Google Sheets, and a custom live view we build for you if you want one. Major redrafts are part of the engagement rather than an extra: when someone goes on leave, changes rotation or leaves mid-year, we rebuild around the gap. For the specifics, see our page on what we build for programs already on Amion. We build to your rules and requests, however granular, with the ACGME requirements among them.

2. Excel / Google Sheets

Model: Manual

If you are looking at alternatives, this is the thing you are most likely moving from, so it should be ranked rather than mentioned in passing. A spreadsheet accepts every rule, every exception and every late request without anyone's permission. Sheets handles two chiefs editing at once and keeps a history of what changed.

Schedule handling is entirely manual, and so is compliance. Nothing watches the 80-hour average, the rest interval or the day off in seven. The operator burden is the highest on this list, and it resets every time the person who understood the file finishes their year.

3. QGenda

Model: Enterprise scheduling platform

QGenda is a well-known healthcare scheduling platform and often comes up as an Amion alternative at the enterprise level. It offers real-time schedule visibility, mobile access, and integration with payroll and credentialing systems.

  • ACGME Rules: Configured by the program. QGenda supports custom rule-building, and your team sets up the duty hour rules and your specialty's details, which takes familiarity with both the platform and your requirements.
  • Compliance Checks: Requires Human Audit. QGenda can flag potential violations based on the rules you've configured, but only if those rules were correctly set up in the first place. Reviewing the result stays with the chief or coordinator.
  • Schedule Handling: Rules-based scheduling run by your team, plus real-time visibility, mobile access and management of the published schedule.

QGenda suits large health systems that want one platform at scale. For a residency program, plan for the setup and for someone at the program to run it and review the output.

4. Lightning Bolt (by PerfectServe)

Model: Self-service scheduling software

Lightning Bolt is a physician scheduling platform that has been adopted by some residency programs looking for more automation than a basic calendar tool provides. It sits in the middle of the spectrum, more automated than a basic calendar, but still firmly a self-service product.

  • ACGME Rules: User-Configurable. Users can program scheduling rules into the system, and Lightning Bolt does offer rule-based generation. How far that goes for your specialty's rules is worth testing on your own schedule during a demo.
  • Compliance Checks: Requires Manual Audits. The tool generates from your rules, and a person at the program reviews the output before it goes out.
  • Schedule Handling: Rules-Based Generation. It offers more automation than a publishing platform, but the user remains in the driver's seat for resolving conflicts, adjusting for fairness, and verifying compliance.

A step up from a blank spreadsheet for programs with someone to run it; the operator role stays with the program.

5. New Innovations

Model: Residency Management Suite

New Innovations is a broad GME management platform covering evaluations, case logs, duty hour logging, procedure tracking and curriculum management. Scheduling is one of several modules within a larger suite.

  • ACGME Rules: Built for the GME environment, with duty hour logging that programs use to monitor the rules.
  • Compliance Checks: Logged hours are reviewed by the program after the fact.
  • Schedule Handling: Rotation and call schedules are entered and managed by the program in the scheduling module.

New Innovations is a strong GME administrative hub (evaluations, milestones, case logs, duty hours). Building the call schedule itself is still the program's work.

Who Builds the Schedule

With four of the five options here, the chief resident or program coordinator still operates the tool. They can reduce manual work, but someone still has to know the rules, configure them correctly, and audit the output.

That's not a knock on the tools individually. QGenda delivers real operational value for enterprise health systems. New Innovations is a legitimate administrative backbone for many GME offices. But if the question is "who builds my call schedule to the ACGME requirements so I am not auditing every line?", the answer with a self-service tool is still your team.

So the deciding question is who does the build.

With every option here except Scheduling Wizard, it is you.

With Scheduling Wizard, it is our team: the requirements you tell us apply go into the schedule while it is built, and the review at the end is a check, not a repair job. And because it is a managed service, the chief resident avoids becoming a software expert and does not rebuild the rule set after rotation.

As one resident put it: "there must be a solution for this!!" The fix is taking the build, and the checking, off the chief.
